title: Triples Within Three Gap Limits
statement:
You get an array arr and three limits a, b and c. Count the index triples i < j < k where all three gaps are small enough:

  • |arr[i] − arr[j]| ≤ a
  • |arr[j] − arr[k]| ≤ b
  • |arr[i] − arr[k]| ≤ c

The indices must be in increasing order, but the values can be in any order.

examples.why: Only indices (0, 2, 3) work: values 4, 3, 2 give gaps 1, 1 and 2. Any triple using the 1 has a first gap that is too large.
All gaps are 0, so every choice of three indices counts: 4 of them.
The limit c compares the first and third values directly (1 and 1), regardless of the 9 between them.

hints: With at most 100 values, how many triples are there in total? Is checking all of them fast enough?
Three nested loops with i < j < k, checking the three gaps, is the expected answer. Skip the k loop early when the (i, j) gap already fails.
For a faster version, fix j and k. The valid arr[i] values form one range of numbers, and a running count of values seen before j answers 'how many fall in this range' with a prefix sum.

explain.intuition:
With n ≤ 100 there are at most about 160 000 triples, so trying all of them is the intended solution. The only care needed is to keep i < j < k and to check all three gaps, including the one between i and k, which skips over j.

A faster idea, useful if n grows: fix the pair (j, k). The conditions on arr[i] become two value ranges, [arr[j] − a, arr[j] + a] and [arr[k] − c, arr[k] + c]. Their overlap is one range. Keep a count of every value at indices before j as a prefix-sum table over values, and read off how many fall into the overlap in O(1).
steps: If |arr[i] − arr[j]| > a, skip to the next j.
Otherwise count each k where both |arr[j] − arr[k]| ≤ b and |arr[i] − arr[k]| ≤ c.
pitfalls: Forgetting the third condition between i and k, which is not implied by the other two.
Sorting the array first. The order of indices matters, so sorting changes which triples exist.
Using < instead of ≤: a gap exactly equal to the limit is allowed.

solutions.title: Check every triple
solutions.idea: Three loops in index order, with an early skip when the first gap already fails.

solutions.title: Fix j and k, count i with a value prefix sum
solutions.idea: For a pair (j, k), valid arr[i] values form one range. A prefix-count table over values of the elements before j answers how many fall in it.

followups: n grows to 10 000. The second solution is O(n²); how would a Fenwick tree replace the O(V) prefix update?
Count pairs i < j with |arr[i] − arr[j]| ≤ a in O(n log n).
